title: File a small claims or other civil case in General District Court
question: Someone owes me money. How do I file a small claims or civil case in the Staunton General District Court?
office: Staunton General District Court, Clerk's Office (25th Judicial District): civil and small claims
summary: Sue in the Staunton General District Court (113 E. Beverley St., 1st floor) if the person who owes you lives, works or does business in Staunton, or the debt arose here. Claims up to $5,000 can go to the small claims division on Form DC-402, where each side speaks for itself; larger claims use a Warrant in Debt (DC-412). Filing costs about $50 ($36 court fee, $10 legal aid fee, and Staunton's $2 courthouse and $2 law library assessments; confirm with the clerk), plus $12 per defendant the sheriff serves; you can ask for a fee waiver. Civil cases are heard on the 2nd and 4th Fridays. Appeals go to the Circuit Court within 10 days.

legal_basis.citation: Staunton City Code § 3.05.080(1) (Assessment of special court costs; on eCode360, paraphrased in fees and caveats, not quoted)

legal_basis.quote: First continuance granted by Clerk; subsequent requests by Judge on motion.

steps.step: Decide whether the claim goes to small claims or to the regular civil docket
steps.who: Plaintiff (the person or business that is owed money)
steps.how: Small claims division: a claim for money, or to get back specific personal property, worth up to $5,000 (interest not counted). Use Warrant in Debt - Small Claims Division (DC-402) for money, or Warrant in Detinue - Small Claims Division (DC-404) for property. Each side speaks for itself, except that a business may send an owner, general partner, officer, member or employee; a party the judge finds unable to understand or take part in the hearing may be represented by a friend or relative who knows the facts and is not a lawyer; and a lawyer may appear only for himself or to move the case out of small claims. Regular civil docket of the General District Court: claims up to $4,500 can be filed only in a general district court, and claims over $4,500 up to $50,000 can be filed here or in the Circuit Court (Warrant in Debt, DC-412); lawyers may appear and the formal rules apply. A claim up to $5,000 may go on either docket. Small claims cannot hear Virginia Tort Claims Act suits against the Commonwealth or claims against state officers or employees over their official duties.
steps.quote: the small claims court shall have jurisdiction, concurrent with that of the general district court, over the civil action specified in § 16.1-77 (1) when the amount claimed does not exceed $5,000, exclusive of interest.

steps.step: Check that the claim is not too old to bring
steps.how: Each kind of claim has a time limit (statute of limitations) that runs from when the claim arose. For money owed under a written contract signed by the person you are suing, it is five years; for an oral or implied agreement, or a written one the other side did not sign, it is three years. A suit on such a contract to collect a medical debt must be started within three years from the due date of the final invoice for the health care service, unless a payment plan allows longer (Va. Code § 8.01-246(B)). A claim for damage to property has five years (Va. Code § 8.01-243(B)), and a claim for personal injury or fraud two years. The court's pamphlet warns that some claims have much shorter limits, so file as soon as you can. The case counts as started when the papers are filed and the fee paid, but that start is void if the warrant is never served and returned to the court.
steps.deadline: Five years for a written contract signed by the defendant; three years for an unwritten contract or one the defendant did not sign; counted from when the claim arose (medical debt: three years from the final invoice's due date)
steps.quote: In actions on any contract that is not otherwise specified and that is in writing and signed by the party to be charged thereby, or by his agent, within five years whether such writing be under seal or not;

steps.step: Check that Staunton is the right court
steps.how: File in the Staunton General District Court if the defendant lives or mainly works in the City of Staunton, if a business defendant has its principal office, place of business or registered agent in the city, or if the claim, or part of it, arose in the city. Augusta County, which surrounds Staunton, has its own general district court (100 Dick Huff Lane, Suite 1070, Verona), and Waynesboro has a separate one too; a case that belongs in one of them should be filed there. If a case is filed in the wrong place, the defendant can object in writing on or before the trial date, and the court transfers the case to a proper court instead of dismissing it.
steps.quote: The simplest rule is that you bring suit in the city or county where the defendant lives, is regularly employed, or has a regular place of business.

steps.step: Find the defendant's exact legal name and a street address for service
steps.how: Use a home street address if you can; a work address will do, but then the warrant must be handed to the defendant in person. Give the city or county, ZIP code and any apartment number. For a business trading under an assumed name, check the fictitious name statement filed with the Circuit Court Clerk and sue the owner 'trading as' the business name. For a corporation or LLC, look up its registered agent with the State Corporation Commission (https://scc.virginia.gov/). A post office box alone will not do.
steps.quote: A post office box number alone is insufficient for service.

steps.step: Fill in the warrant in debt
steps.who: Plaintiff (for a business: an officer, manager or general partner, or an employee or agent the business authorizes in writing)
steps.how: Small claims: Warrant in Debt - Small Claims Division (DC-402). Regular docket: Warrant in Debt (DC-412), which also has a line for attorney's fees. Enter 'Staunton' as the General District Court with its street address (113 E. Beverley St., 1st Floor, Staunton, VA 24401-4390), the names and addresses of the plaintiff and each defendant, the amount owed net of any credits, any interest rate and the date it runs from, and the basis of the claim (open account, contract, note or other), answer the form's 'Homestead exemption waived?' box, then date and sign. The clerk adds the return date, the case number and the issuing signature. Bring the original, one copy for each defendant and one for yourself; the court also recommends an extra copy to mail to the defendant (step s10). The forms can be completed online at vacourts.gov and printed. A business may prepare, sign and file these papers without a lawyer.
steps.quote: If the plaintiff is seeking only a money judgment, he or she should prepare and file a warrant in debt (Form DC-402 Warrant in Debt - Small Claims Division)

steps.step: File the warrant with the Clerk's Office and pay the fees
steps.who: Plaintiff, at the Staunton General District Court Clerk's Office
steps.how: Take the completed warrant and copies to the Clerk's Office, 113 E. Beverley St., 1st Floor (open 8:30 am to 4:30 pm; phone (540) 332-3878). The court pamphlet says a magistrate can also issue a warrant. Pay the filing fee and the sheriff's fee for each defendant. The pieces are a $36 state court fee; a $10 legal aid fee where a nonprofit legal aid program serves the city; Staunton's $2.00 courthouse assessment and $2.00 law library assessment on each civil action (City Code §§ 3.05.080 and 2.75.060); and $12 for each defendant the sheriff serves. Get the exact total from the state's Civil Filing Fee Calculation (choose 'Staunton General District') or by calling the civil section of the Clerk's Office. The state self-help site says filing fees are paid in cash, by certified check or by money order. Court staff can explain procedure but cannot give legal advice.
steps.fee: About $50 if every listed fee applies ($36 court fee, $10 legal aid fee, $2.00 courthouse and $2.00 law library assessments), plus $12 for each defendant served by the sheriff; total not confirmed with the court (see fees and caveats)
steps.quote: At the time of filing a small claims civil warrant, the plaintiff shall pay to the clerk a required fee, which will be taxed as costs in the case.

steps.step: If you cannot afford the fees, ask the judge to waive them
steps.who: A plaintiff who lives in Virginia, or any defendant; a judge decides
steps.how: File the Petition for Proceeding in Civil Case Without Payment of Fees or Costs (DC-409) with your papers; the state self-help site links the same petition on the circuit court form, CC-1414, and says to ask the court about its procedure. You are presumed unable to pay if you receive public assistance (such as TANF, Medicaid, Supplemental Security Income or SNAP) or have a legal aid or pro bono lawyer, though the court can look more closely at your finances and find otherwise. Otherwise the judge adds your net income and liquid assets, subtracts exceptional expenses such as medical costs, support payments and child care, and presumes you unable to pay if the result is at or below 125 percent of the federal poverty guidelines for your household. The state's fee calculator page says to contact the court about the proof of indigency it needs. If the petition is granted, the court officers serve your papers without fees.
steps.deadline: When you file (or, for a defendant, when you defend)
steps.fee: None if the petition is granted
steps.quote: and who is on account of his poverty unable to pay fees or costs, may be allowed by a court to sue or defend a suit therein, without paying fees or costs;

steps.step: Set the return (court) date with the clerk
steps.who: Plaintiff, with the agreement of the Clerk's Office
steps.how: In small claims the plaintiff chooses the hearing date, subject to the clerk's agreement, and it must be at least five days after the defendant is served. The court's page lists the Staunton civil docket on the 2nd and 4th Fridays, with returns at 9:00 a.m. and contested cases at 11:00 a.m.; it lists no separate small claims time, so ask the clerk which docket and time apply. State law says the return date can be no more than 90 days after service. The chief judge may limit how many cases one person sets for trial on one day.
steps.deadline: At least five days, and no more than 90 days, after service
steps.quote: The plaintiff shall select a time for the hearing which shall be held at least five days after service of the warrant.

steps.who: The Staunton City Sheriff's Office (for an address in the city), the sheriff where the defendant lives, or a private process server
steps.how: The clerk sends the warrant to the sheriff of the city or county where the defendant is; in Staunton that is the Staunton City Sheriff's Office. Instead, any adult who is not a party and has no interest in the case, such as a private process server, can serve it and then file proof of service on DC-411. Service is made by handing the warrant to the defendant in person; if the defendant is not found at home, by leaving it there with a family member aged 16 or older (not a temporary visitor or guest) and explaining what it is; and only if neither can be done, by posting it on the front or main door of the home. If the server cannot find the defendant, the warrant comes back 'not found' and the case cannot be tried until the defendant is served; the clerk can reissue it once, within three months of the original return day, at no charge.
steps.deadline: At least five days before the return day
steps.fee: $12 for each defendant served by a Virginia sheriff
steps.quote: Service of the warrant shall be made as provided in Chapter 8 (§ 8.01-285 et seq.) of Title 8.01, but the warrant must be served not less than five days before the return day.

steps.step: Mail a copy to each defendant and file a certificate of mailing (required before a default judgment if the warrant was posted)
steps.who: Plaintiff (or the plaintiff's employee or agent)
steps.how: The law requires this only when the warrant is served by posting it on the defendant's door: the court will not enter a default judgment until you show you mailed a copy at least 10 days earlier; otherwise the case is continued. The state's Small Claims Court Procedures guide and self-help page recommend it in every case: send a copy of the warrant to each defendant by first-class mail at least 10 days before the first court date, and fill in the certificate of mailing (on the back of DC-402, or Form DC-413). Give it to the judge at trial or file it with the clerk before the trial date. In general district court, mailing the warrant (showing the return date, time and place) before or after filing meets the mailing rule.
steps.deadline: At least 10 days before a default judgment can be entered on posted service (recommended: at least 10 days before the first court date)
steps.quote: provided that not less than 10 days before judgment by default may be entered, the party causing service or his attorney or agent mails to the party served a copy of such process and thereafter files in the office of the clerk of the court a certificate of such mailing.

steps.who: Either party, through the Clerk's Office
steps.how: File a Request for Witness Subpoena (DC-325) with the clerk, giving each witness's name and current home address, and pay the sheriff's fee for each one. The witness must receive the subpoena at least five days before trial; if a properly subpoenaed witness whose testimony matters does not come, the judge will usually continue the case if you ask. Tell your witnesses before they are served.
steps.deadline: At least ten days before the trial date
steps.fee: $12 sheriff's fee for each witness served
steps.quote: In order to ensure the presence of your witnesses, you should ask the clerk of the court for a subpoena at least ten days in advance of the hearing day.

steps.how: You do not have to come to court, but if you do not, judgment may be entered against you. To dispute the claim, come on the return date. You may file a written counterclaim before trial (in small claims, up to $5,000). On the regular docket the judge may order the plaintiff to file a bill of particulars and you to file grounds of defense (DC-441, DC-442) by set dates. If the case was filed in the wrong city or county, file a written venue objection with the clerk before the trial date, or give it to the judge when the case is called, and send a copy to the plaintiff. In small claims you may move the case to the regular General District Court docket, where lawyers can appear, at any time before the judge decides, using the removal notice on the back of the warrant; a lawyer may appear for you just to do that. You can also ask for a fee waiver (step s7). If your address changes, tell the clerk and the other side in writing (DC-437).
steps.deadline: Counterclaim before trial; venue objection on or before the day of trial; removal before the judge decides
steps.fee: A counterclaim may carry a filing fee; ask the clerk
steps.quote: TO DEFENDANT: You are not required to appear; however, if you fail to appear, judgment may be entered against you.

steps.step: If the defendant does not come: ask for a default judgment
steps.how: If a properly served defendant does not appear, the judge may enter a default judgment for the plaintiff on enough evidence to support the claim. Before that, file the Servicemembers Civil Relief Act affidavit (DC-418), stating whether the defendant is in military service and the facts that show it, or that you cannot tell; if the court cannot tell either, it may require you to post a bond first. If the warrant was posted on the door, also show the certificate of mailing (step s10). If the plaintiff does not come, the defendant may ask the judge to rule for the defendant.
steps.quote: the court shall not enter a judgment by default until the plaintiff files with the court an affidavit (i) stating whether or not the defendant is in military service and showing necessary facts to support the affidavit;

steps.step: Go to court on the return date
steps.who: Both parties; a Staunton General District Court judge decides
steps.how: Come to 113 E. Beverley St. at the date and time on the warrant; the court's page says cell phones are not allowed in the building. Small claims: by law the case is tried on the first return date unless all parties agree to another date or the court orders one, and other continuances need good cause (the court's posted policy that the clerk grants a first continuance is discussed in caveats). Witnesses are sworn, the hearing is informal, and the judge may admit any useful evidence except privileged communications. Bring the contract, invoices, receipts, messages and photos, with copies for the judge and the other side. You must prove both that you should win and how much is owed. Regular docket: if the defendant appears and disputes the claim, the judge may set a later trial date (the court lists contested civil cases at 11:00 a.m. on the civil Fridays).
steps.deadline: The return date and time on the warrant
steps.quote: The trial shall be conducted on the first return date.

steps.step: After judgment: interest, a new trial, or setting aside a default
steps.who: Either party; the judge who decided the case
steps.how: A money judgment carries interest at six percent a year, or at the contract rate if that is higher on a contract claim. A motion for a new trial (DC-368, Motion for New Trial (Civil)) must be made within 30 days after the judgment, and the court must rule within 45 days of the judgment. Separately, on motion of the plaintiff or the judgment debtor (DC-434) and after reasonable notice to the other side, the court may set aside a default judgment for fraud on the court (within two years), because the judgment is void, because the debt was already settled (accord and satisfaction), or because the defendant was a servicemember. The new-trial statute says it does not alter the requirements for an appeal, so the 10-day appeal deadline in step s16 still runs from the judgment; no source read here says a motion to set aside a default extends it either.
steps.deadline: New trial: within 30 days after the date of judgment, not counting that day; set aside for fraud on the court: within two years of the judgment
steps.quote: No new trial may be granted from any judgment in a district court unless a motion by one of the parties is made within thirty days after the date of judgment, not including the date of entry of such judgment.

steps.step: Appeal to the Staunton Circuit Court
steps.who: The losing party, by notice to the General District Court clerk; the Staunton Circuit Court hears the appeal
steps.how: If more than $20 is in controversy (not counting interest, attorney fees provided for in the contract, and costs), file a notice of appeal with the General District Court clerk within 10 days of the judgment (Civil Appeal Notice, DC-475, available from the clerk's office; it is not posted online). Within 30 days of the judgment, post the appeal bond the court sets (Civil Appeal Bond, DC-460) and pay the General District Court clerk the Circuit Court writ tax and costs, including the fee for serving the notice of appeal; the papers then go to the Circuit Court, whose clerk dockets the appeal and notifies the other side, and the appeal is not heard unless that notice was given (or waived) at least 10 days before the trial date. A plaintiff who faced no counterclaim, and a defendant found indigent, need not post a bond. The Staunton Circuit Court (113 East Beverley Street; Clerk's Office on the third floor) tries the case again from the start under the formal rules; either side may ask for a jury if more than $50 is in controversy. Its page says civil cases are set by praecipe submitted not more than 28 or less than 7 days before Motion Day (the 2nd Tuesday of each month, 9:00 a.m.).
steps.deadline: Notice within 10 days of judgment; bond, writ tax and costs within 30 days of judgment
steps.fee: $5 writ tax and the $100 Circuit Court clerk's fee (claims up to $49,999), the fee for serving the notice of appeal, and any bond (see fees)
steps.quote: Notice of the appeal must be filed in the general district court where the case was heard within ten days after the judgment is entered.

steps.step: Collect a money judgment that is not paid
steps.who: Judgment creditor (the winner), through the General District Court clerk; the sheriff levies
steps.how: A judgment does not collect itself. From 21 days after the judgment, the clerk will issue on request a writ of fieri facias, which is a lien on the debtor's personal property; the sheriff can levy on property you point out (you post a bond with the sheriff before property is seized and sold). With it you can (a) have the debtor summoned to answer questions about assets (Summons to Answer Interrogatories, DC-440), certifying that you have not done so against that debtor in the past six months; or (b) garnish wages or a bank account (Suggestion for Summons in Garnishment, DC-450; both the debtor and the garnishee, usually the employer or bank, are served), subject to the exemptions the debtor can claim. For a garnishment you give the debtor's last known address, give the clerk (when the sheriff serves) a stamped envelope addressed to the debtor, and give the debtor's social security number, or state that you tried in good faith and could not get it (Va. Code § 8.01-511(B)). Separately, (c) you can get an abstract of judgment and record it in a circuit court clerk's office as a lien on the debtor's real estate in that city or county. A general district court judgment can be enforced for 10 years from its date.
steps.deadline: Writ of fieri facias available 21 days after the judgment; no execution after 10 years from the judgment
steps.fee: $36 court fee for each interrogatory summons or garnishment, plus $12 for each party the sheriff serves; $25 sheriff's fee to levy an execution
steps.quote: to issue a writ of fieri facias at the expiration of twenty-one days from the date of the entry of the judgment

steps.step: When the judgment is paid, have it marked satisfied
steps.who: Judgment creditor; if the creditor does not act, the debtor by motion
steps.how: The creditor must file a written notice of satisfaction (DC-458) with the clerk, giving the case number, the parties and the date of judgment, within 30 days of receiving payment. If the creditor does not, the debtor can give the creditor 10 days' notice and move the court (DC-459) to mark the judgment satisfied; the court may order the creditor to pay the costs, including reasonable attorney fees.
steps.quote: When satisfaction of any judgment rendered in a court not of record is made, the judgment creditor shall by himself, or his agent or attorney, give written notice of such satisfaction, within 30 days of receipt, to the clerk of the court in which the judgment was rendered.

escalation.trigger: You need a new court date
escalation.next: The Staunton General District Court Clerk's Office for a first continuance under the court's posted policy; a judge, on motion, for any later request (in small claims, only on good cause or with all parties' consent)
escalation.quote: A continuance shall be granted to either the plaintiff or defendant only upon good cause shown.

escalation.trigger: You cannot pay the filing and service fees
escalation.next: A Staunton General District Court judge, on a Petition for Proceeding in Civil Case Without Payment of Fees or Costs (DC-409)
escalation.quote: and who is on account of his poverty unable to pay fees or costs, may be allowed by a court to sue or defend a suit therein, without paying fees or costs;

escalation.trigger: Both sides might settle the dispute without a trial
escalation.next: Court-referred mediation orientation (the state's mediation coordinator list names a contractor for the Staunton General District Court; ask the clerk)
escalation.quote: a court, on its own motion or on motion of one of the parties, may refer any contested civil matter, or selected issues in a civil matter, to an orientation session in order to encourage the early resolution of disputes

escalation.trigger: Defendant in small claims wants a lawyer or the formal rules of the regular court
escalation.next: The regular civil docket of the Staunton General District Court (removal)
escalation.deadline: Before the judge hands down a decision
escalation.quote: A defendant shall have the right to remove the case to the general district court at any point preceding the handing down of the decision by the judge and may be represented by an attorney for that purpose.

escalation.trigger: The case was filed in the wrong city or county
escalation.next: The court rules on the defendant's written venue objection and transfers the case to a proper court (for example the Augusta General District Court)
escalation.deadline: On or before the day of trial
escalation.quote: As to actions in general district courts, a motion objecting to venue, which may be in the form of a letter or other written communication, shall be filed with or received by the court on or before the day of trial.

escalation.trigger: Judgment entered against you and you have grounds for a new trial
escalation.next: The judge who entered the judgment, on a motion for new trial (DC-368)
escalation.deadline: Within 30 days after the date of judgment
escalation.quote: No new trial may be granted from any judgment in a district court unless a motion by one of the parties is made within thirty days after the date of judgment, not including the date of entry of such judgment.

escalation.trigger: A default judgment was obtained by fraud on the court, is void, covers a debt already settled, or was entered against a servicemember
escalation.next: Staunton General District Court, on a Motion to Set Aside Default Judgment (DC-434)
escalation.deadline: Within two years of the judgment for fraud on the court
escalation.quote: Such motion on the ground of fraud on the court shall be made within two years from the date of the judgment or decree.

escalation.trigger: You lost at trial and more than $20 is in controversy
escalation.next: Staunton Circuit Court: a new trial from the start (de novo), with a jury on request if more than $50 is in controversy
escalation.deadline: Notice within 10 days of judgment; bond, writ tax and costs within 30 days
escalation.quote: there shall be an appeal of right, if taken within 10 days after such order or judgment, to a court of record.

escalation.trigger: You lost the appeal in the Circuit Court
escalation.next: Court of Appeals of Virginia (appeal of right from a final civil judgment of a circuit court, Va. Code § 17.1-405(A)(3))
escalation.deadline: Notice of appeal within 30 days of the final judgment
escalation.quote: a notice of appeal to the Court of Appeals in any case within the jurisdiction of the court shall be filed within 30 days from the date of any final judgment order, decree, or conviction.

escalation.trigger: The defendant ignores the money judgment
escalation.next: Staunton General District Court Clerk: writ of fieri facias, summons to answer interrogatories and garnishment summons; the sheriff levies
escalation.deadline: From 21 days after the judgment, while the judgment remains enforceable (10 years)
escalation.quote: a summons in the form prescribed by § 8.01-512.3 may be sued out of the clerk's office (i) of the court from which an execution on the judgment is issued so long as the judgment shall remain enforceable as provided in § 8.01-251

escalation.trigger: The judgment was paid but the creditor did not file a notice of satisfaction within 30 days
escalation.next: Staunton General District Court, on the debtor's Motion for Judgment to be Marked Satisfied (DC-459)
escalation.deadline: After giving the creditor 10 days' notice
escalation.quote: the judgment debtor, his heirs or personal representatives, may, on motion, after 10 days' notice thereof to the judgment creditor, or his assignee, his personal representative, or his agent or attorney, apply to the court in which the judgment was rendered to have the judgment marked satisfied.

escalation.trigger: A disability accommodation is refused, or you have an accessibility complaint about the court
escalation.next: Accommodation requests in a pending case go first to the Staunton General District Court clerk. A complaint about the General District Court is handled under the grievance procedures of the Office of the Executive Secretary of the Supreme Court of Virginia, available through its ADA Coordinator; only complaints about a circuit court clerk's office go to that clerk
escalation.basis: Notice Regarding the Americans with Disabilities Act, Virginia's Judicial System (https://www.vacourts.gov/static/resources/small_claims_court_procedures.pdf)
escalation.quote: Other complaints will be handled pursuant to grievance procedures adopted by the Office of the Executive Secretary.

escalation.trigger: Misconduct by a judge (not disagreement with a ruling, which is appealed)
escalation.quote: to investigate charges arising out of the present or any prior term of office which would be the basis for retirement, censure, or removal of a judge

caveats: Filing fee total not confirmed. The state's Civil Filing Fee Calculation (https://www.vacourts.gov/gdfees_calc_app) lists 'Staunton General District' but works only by submitting a form, so its result is not given here. The roughly $50 figure is lexflow's arithmetic from these pieces: the $36 court fee (Va. Code § 16.1-69.48:2), the $10 legal aid fee (§ 17.1-278), and the $2.00 courthouse and $2.00 law library assessments in Staunton City Code §§ 3.05.080(1) and 2.75.060; the sheriff adds $12 per defendant (§ 17.1-272(A)). The state's fee help page separately says a court-specific Courthouse Construction Fee is charged per case on claims of $500.01 to $50,000; whether that is the city's $2.00 assessment or something more (for example the additional local assessment of up to $3 allowed by § 17.1-281(C)) was not confirmed. Call the civil section of the Clerk's Office or use the calculator.

The $10 legal aid fee applies only where a nonprofit legal aid program under the Virginia State Bar provides free civil representation in the locality (§ 17.1-278). No official page read here confirms that for Staunton.

City Code. Staunton's code is on General Code's eCode360, whose Terms and Conditions of Use limit content to personal use and forbid reproducing it for public purposes, so no City Code text is quoted. The paraphrases here rest on the code's table of contents, Chapter 3.05 (§ 3.05.080, https://ecode360.com/49100121) and Chapter 2.75 (§ 2.75.060, https://ecode360.com/49100028), consulted for reference only. In paraphrase: § 3.05.080(1) assesses $2.00 as costs in each civil action filed in the Staunton general district, juvenile and domestic relations district and circuit courts, collected by the clerk for courthouse and jail construction, renovation and maintenance; § 2.75.060 assesses $2.00 as costs in each civil action filed in the city's circuit and general district courts, for the Staunton-Augusta Law Library, except actions where the Commonwealth, a political subdivision or the federal government is a party and costs are assessed against it. eCode360 says its codes may not reflect the latest legislation; the city's official copy was not consulted.

The City of Staunton's website (www.ci.staunton.va.us) refuses automated readers, and no city page on civil process service is cited, so the Sheriff's civil process practice in Staunton is described only from the statewide guides. The Staunton City Sheriff's Office phone and address are those on the Internet Archive copy of the Sheriff's page of 17 July 2026 (the live city site refuses automated readers); check them before you rely on them.

Docket. The court's vacourts.gov page lists Civil on the 2nd and 4th Fridays (Returns 9:00 a.m., Contested 11:00 a.m.) and no separate small claims docket. Which time a small claims case is set for, and whether the clerk sets small claims trials on the return docket, was not found; ask the clerk. The return date on the warrant controls.

Continuances. The court's page says 'First continuance granted by Clerk; subsequent requests by Judge on motion.' For small claims, Va. Code § 16.1-122.3(E) says the trial is held on the first return date unless all parties consent or the court orders a change, and any other continuance needs good cause. How the clerk's first-continuance policy applies to small claims cases is not stated; ask the clerk.

Dollar limits differ between sources. The index text of Va. Code § 16.1-77 (history through 2025, c. 338) gives exclusive jurisdiction up to $4,500 and concurrent jurisdiction up to $50,000 for all claims in subdivision (1). The vacourts.gov General District Court page says $4,500 and $25,000, with up to $50,000 only for personal injury and wrongful death, and the General District Courts pamphlet (6/2021) says $25,000. The fee calculator's claim box runs to $50,000.00. The small claims limit of $5,000 (§ 16.1-122.2) is the same everywhere. Confirm a claim over $25,000 with the clerk.

Return date limit: the DC-402 instructions (September 2008) say the return date cannot exceed sixty days from service, but Va. Code § 16.1-79 (amended 2025, c. 349) says 90 days. This page follows the statute; the clerk sets the date in practice.

Jury threshold on appeal: Va. Code § 16.1-113 allows a jury if more than fifty dollars is in controversy. The Small Claims Court Procedures PDF says a jury may be requested if the claim exceeds $20, and the state self-help page says $100. This page follows the statute.

The Civil Appeal Notice (DC-475) is not posted online (https://www.vacourts.gov/static/forms/district/dc475.pdf returned HTTP 404 on 2026-10-11); the Small Claims Court Procedures PDF and the self-help page say it is used for filing an appeal and is available from the General District Court clerk's office. It is named in step s16 but not listed under forms.

Two fee-waiver forms exist: DC-409 on the district civil forms list, and CC-1414 (revised 07/26), which the state self-help page points to. Both cite Va. Code §§ 16.1-69.48:4 and 17.1-606. Ask the clerk which one this court uses, and what proof of indigency it wants.
Payment methods: only the state self-help site states them (cash, certified check or money order). No Staunton General District Court page says which methods its civil section accepts.

Statutes of limitation: the contract periods (§ 8.01-246(A)), the three-year medical debt rule (§ 8.01-246(B)), the personal injury and fraud period (§ 8.01-243(A)) and the five-year property damage period (§ 8.01-243(B)) are quoted. Tolling and extensions (for example time while a defendant obstructs filing, or a new written promise to pay, § 8.01-229(D) and (G)) are not covered. Other claims (for example on a dishonoured check, under the Uniform Commercial Code, or against a government body) can have different periods and notice rules, which are not covered here.

Mediation. The state's Mediation Coordinator Contractors list (https://www.vacourts.gov/static/courtadmin/aoc/djs/programs/drs/mediation/resources/coordinator_contracts_court.pdf) names the Fairfield Center as the mediation coordinator for the Staunton General District Court. The contact persons and phone numbers on that list are not recorded (individuals' names, and the phone column does not line up with the rows in the PDF text). Whether the Staunton court refers small claims cases to mediation in practice was not found; the mediation page says to contact the court's mediation coordinator or the clerk's office.

Not covered here: detinue (return of property) procedure beyond naming DC-404; the fee for filing a counterclaim in General District Court; garnishment exemptions and the exemption hearing (DC-407, DC-454, Va. Code § 8.01-512.4); interest before judgment (Va. Code § 8.01-382); the amount of the levy bond the sheriff requires; Circuit Court costs beyond the writ tax and clerk's fee on appeal; e-filing for general district court civil cases; interpreter requests for spoken languages; unlawful detainer (eviction) and tenant cases, which the same court hears.

The step on default judgment after posted service, and the advice to mail a copy at least 10 days before the first court date, come from the Small Claims Court Procedures PDF and the state self-help page; the rule itself is quoted from Va. Code § 8.01-296(2)(b).

The Small Claims Court Procedures PDF and the self-help page give different State Corporation Commission phone numbers for finding a registered agent ((804) 371-9733 or 1-866-722-2551, and (804) 371-9967), so none is recorded; step s4 points to the SCC website named in the General District Courts pamphlet.

Privacy: the court pages name the General District Court clerk, the Circuit Court clerk and the judges; no names are recorded. The phone (540) 332-3878 and fax (540) 332-3985 are the numbers vacourts.gov publishes in the court's contact block with its hours and address, below the clerk's name, so they are recorded as the Clerk's Office lines; the same applies to the Circuit Court's (540) 332-3874. Judges' chambers lines, the ADA Coordinator's name, the mediation contractor's contact persons, and the Sheriff's Office mailbox are left out. No email address for the Staunton General District Court was found.
The General District Court Case Information system (eapps.courts.state.va.us) and the fee calculator were not used; they are listed as published on the vacourts.gov pages.

Statute versions: Va. Code § 16.1-94.1 (10-year enforcement of district court judgments) was amended in 2026 (c. 848), § 16.1-107 in 2026 (c. 579) and § 8.01-511 in 2026 (cc. 637, 638); Open US Law's copy holds those versions. No section quoted here is marked there with an end date. Under the amended § 16.1-94.1, a plaintiff can avoid the 10-year bar by docketing the judgment in the circuit court only for judgments entered before July 1, 2026; step 17's 10-year limit is stated for judgments entered now. Whether a newer judgment can be extended under § 8.01-251 is not settled here.

Scope: this page covers only the Staunton General District Court. A defendant in Augusta County or Waynesboro is sued in that locality's own general district court; the Augusta court's civil docket (1st and 3rd Mondays, per its vacourts.gov page) and Waynesboro's are not covered here.

removed: Escalation rung 12 (disability access): the ADA notice sentence 'A request for accommodation should be made to the relevant clerk if the request relates to a pending case or activity of a particular court.' Confirmed word for word in the Small Claims Court Procedures PDF, but it is about requests, not the rung's trigger (a refused accommodation or a complaint). corrections: Quotes: all 116 original quotes confirmed. The 106 state-law quotes (70 legal_basis, 12 step, 12 fee and 12 escalation quotes) are substrings of I.text_of for the cited section with whitespace normalised only, across 44 sections, none marked with an end date, and each cited subsection label matches the text. The 10 local and procedure quotes were matched word for word against pages re-fetched read-only on 2026-10-11: the vacourts.gov Staunton General District Court page, the Small Claims Court Procedures PDF (revision 10/2024), the General District Courts pamphlet (gdinfo.pdf), Form DC-402, gdcivilfeeshelp.html and selfhelp.vacourts.gov /page/11/. robots.txt allows these paths; requests were 2 seconds apart with the lexflow User-Agent; no form was submitted. 13 state-law quotes were added and checked the same way (one more section, § 16.1-112), and one official-page quote was replaced, for 129 in all (119 state, 10 official pages).

Escalation rung 12 (disability access): 'next' sent complaints first to 'the clerk of the court for a pending case'. The ADA notice sends accommodation requests about a pending case to the clerk, sends only complaints about a circuit court clerk's office to that clerk, and handles other complaints, including about the General District Court, under the Office of the Executive Secretary's grievance procedures. 'next' and the quote now say so.

Step s9: listed handing the warrant to the defendant, leaving it with a family member and posting it as equal choices. Va. Code § 8.01-296(2) allows family-member service only when the defendant is not found at home, excludes a temporary sojourner or guest, and allows posting only when that cannot be done. Fixed, with both subdivisions quoted in legal_basis.

Step s10: presented mailing a copy and filing a certificate of mailing as required in every case. § 8.01-296(2)(b) requires it only for posted service, before a default judgment; the Small Claims Court Procedures PDF and the self-help page recommend it in every case, at least 10 days before the first court date. The title, how and deadline now separate what is required from what is recommended.

Step s15: 'Neither motion extends the 10-day appeal deadline' was supported only for the new-trial motion (§ 16.1-97.1(B), now quoted); the text now says so and that no source read says a motion to set aside a default extends it. Added that the § 8.01-428(A) motion is made by the plaintiff or judgment debtor after reasonable notice to the other side (quoted). The deadline now includes the two-year limit for fraud on the court.

Step s16: added that the $20 threshold excludes interest, contracted attorney fees and costs (§ 16.1-106(A), quoted); that the writ tax and costs are paid to the clerk of the court the appeal is taken from, the General District Court clerk (§ 16.1-107(E)); and that the Circuit Court clerk dockets the appeal and the appeal is not heard unless the other side had notice, or waived it, 10 days before trial (§ 16.1-112, quoted).
